sections.heading: Recognizing how much you have given me
sections.text: Eternal God, my Father, your greatness is beyond me, your goodness is deeper than I can understand, and your grace keeps overflowing toward me. I could sooner count every grain of sand along the sea than count all the kindnesses you have shown me. I only notice a small part of what you do, but even that small part is more than enough to fill my mouth with praise.
theological_themes: God's greatness, goodness, and overflowing grace
Human inability to fully grasp or measure God's mercies
Praise as the fitting response to God's generosity

scripture_references.connection: This psalm calls the worshiper to remember the Lord's many benefits, including forgiveness, healing, redemption, steadfast love, and renewal. It supports the prayer's opening movement of noticing that God's mercies are too many and too rich to treat casually.

Paul speaks of redemption and forgiveness according to the riches of God's grace, which he lavishes on his people. That grounds the prayer's confidence that God's grace is not reluctant or thin, but abundant.

sections.heading: Thanking you for ordinary mercies
sections.text: Thank you for the daily gifts I often take for granted: the health I still have, the ways you have protected my body, a place to live, food to eat, clothes to wear, and the continued use of my mind. Thank you for my family, for the help we give one another, for peace at home when you grant it, and for the chairs around the table that are still filled and could have been empty. Thank you for my country, for your church, for the Bible, and for the faith you have given me.
theological_themes: Gratitude for bodily, household, and spiritual provisions
God's providential care in ordinary life
Awareness that continued life and family presence are mercies, not entitlements

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that every good gift comes from the Father, which fits the prayer's thanksgiving for health, home, family, Scripture, and faith as received gifts rather than possessions earned or guaranteed.
Paul says God gives life, breath, and everything else, and that all people live within his appointed care. This supports the prayer's wide gratitude for body, mind, place, and daily provision.

sections.heading: Admitting what my life really says about me
sections.text:
But Father, I cannot thank you honestly without also grieving over my sin. I have been ungrateful. I have been corrupt in ways I do not like to admit. Days that should have been filled with love have added to my guilt. Places where I have lived and worked could testify against the words I have spoken there.

Everything around me and within me exposes me: the daylight that has seen what I did, the darkness that hides nothing from you, the enemy who accuses, your holy angels who have seen my rebellion, your face that sees my secret sins, your righteous law, your Word, my stained conscience, my private life, my public life, my neighbors, and even my own self-knowledge. I will not deny it. I will not make excuses. Father, I have sinned.
theological_themes: Honest confession of sin without excuses
God's complete knowledge of hidden and public sin
The condemning witness of conscience, Scripture, and God's law

scripture_references.connection: David confesses his sin directly before God and refuses to minimize it. This grounds the prayer's plain admission of guilt without self-defense.

Hebrews teaches that no creature is hidden from God's sight and that all are exposed before him. That supports the prayer's sense that neither daylight nor darkness, private life nor public life, can conceal sin from God.
Paul explains that God's law stops every mouth and holds the world accountable before God. This fits the prayer's refusal to argue back or frame excuses when confronted by God's righteous standard.

sections.heading: Running back to you because of Jesus
sections.text: And yet I am still alive, and I come back to you repenting. I run to your open arms because Jesus brings me near. You will not throw me away, because he has made a way for me to come. You will not condemn me, because he died in my place. You will not keep a record of my mountains of sin as though they still stand between us, because he has dealt with them. What is ugly in me is covered by his beauty, and I am received because of him.
theological_themes: Forgiveness and acceptance in Christ rather than personal worthiness

scripture_references.connection: In Jesus' parable, the repentant son returns confessing sin and is received by the father's compassion rather than rejected. This illuminates the prayer's movement from confession to running toward the Father's open arms.

Paul declares that there is no condemnation for those in Christ because God dealt with sin through his Son. This directly supports the prayer's confidence that condemnation has been answered by Christ.

Hebrews presents Jesus as the one who saves completely those who draw near to God through him, because he intercedes for them. That grounds the prayer's statement that Jesus brings the sinner near to God.

sections.heading: Leaving sin by holding to the cross
sections.text: My God, I want to be done with sin, not by trusting my own resolve, but by holding tightly to the cross of Jesus. Let me take shelter in what he suffered for me—his wounds, his pierced side, his death for sinners. Keep me there: humbled, forgiven, protected, and changed.
theological_themes: Renouncing sin through dependence on Christ crucified
The cross as refuge for guilty sinners

scripture_references.connection: Peter connects Christ bearing sins on the cross with believers dying to sin and living to righteousness. This supports the prayer's claim that farewell to sin happens by clinging to Christ's saving death, not by self-reliance.

Paul teaches that union with Christ in his death means believers are no longer to live as slaves to sin. This gives biblical shape to the prayer's desire to leave sin while depending on what Christ has done.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original speaks of a 'cruel accuser who justly charges me' and angels 'provoked to leave me.' I retained the sense of accusation and spiritual witness without overdeveloping angelology or implying that believers are abandoned by good angels, since that point is not stated plainly in Scripture in the same way.

The phrase about Christ's beauty covering the sinner's deformities reflects a strong Reformed/Puritan emphasis on acceptance before God through Christ rather than personal moral beauty. I preserved that substance while avoiding language that would sound merely aesthetic or self-loathing without the gospel context.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'the seats now filled that might have been vacant' as chairs around the table still filled, to keep the concrete image of preserved family life and mortality.

I interpreted the original's movement from universal accusation to 'Father, I have sinned' through the lens of the prodigal son, because the wording intentionally echoes that confession and leads into the Father's open arms.

I translated 'hiding in his wounds, and sheltering in his side' as taking shelter in what Jesus suffered—his wounds, pierced side, and death for sinners—so the image remains concrete while making clear that the refuge is Christ's atoning work, not a devotional practice detached from the cross.
